title: Xylose phosphatase activity of dystroglycan self-regulates its receptor function.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: No data files exist to open. I retrieved the open-access full text (PMC12632563, which paper_context.py missed because PubMed carries two records for this paper: 42594207 and 41279211) and parsed its XML: it contains 0 tables (0 <table-wrap>, 0 <table> elements) and exactly one supplementary item, 'Supplement 1', whose own contents listing in the article reads 'Materials and Methods, Figs. S1 to S7, References (51-58)' - i.e. a methods-and-figures PDF with no Data S or Table S items. The data availability statement reads in full: 'All data are available in the main text or the supplementary materials.' I ran NCBI elink from the PubMed record and got only pubmed-to-pubmed neighbour links: no GEO, SRA, BioProject, BioSample or dbGaP entry. A PDBe text search for 'dystroglycan' in structure titles returned 0 hits, and the text contains 0 mentions of cryo-EM, crystallography, AlphaFold, RNA-seq, MALDI, flow cytometry or HPLC. Europe PMC's supplementaryFiles endpoint timed out on its one attempt; a bioRxiv media HEAD returned no size.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Everything about the experiments themselves: the nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) binding measurements of LARGE1 with phosphorylated versus unphosphorylated xylose substrates, the enzyme assays with the G4Xp-MU and G4X-MU fluorescent sugar substrates, the FAM20B knockdown mouse phenotyping, and the DXDXT/V active-site mutant results. All of these are reported only as figure panels and gel images; I saw no underlying numbers.

a1_downloadable.note: FAIL. There is no dataset to download. The data availability statement is 'All data are available in the main text or the supplementary materials', and the supplementary material is a single PDF of Materials and Methods plus Figures S1-S7. No repository deposit exists anywhere I looked: no GEO, SRA, BioProject, dbGaP (NCBI elink returned only paper-to-paper links), no Protein Data Bank entry (0 hits for 'dystroglycan' in structure titles), no ProteomeXchange or Zenodo/Dryad record. The only machine-readable artefact is the article XML itself.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL, and this is the deeper failure. The article XML contains zero tables, so no column of any kind exists. Any prediction target - phosphatase activity, matriglycan length, laminin binding - would have to be constructed by reading values off gel bands and bar charts in figure images, which is label construction by eye, not a column.

a3_inputs_present.note: FAIL. No input table either. Protein sequences for the dystroglycan N-terminal domain mutants are described in prose in the Methods (e.g. the DXDXT/V motif substitutions) rather than provided as a sequence file, and the sugar substrates are named (G4X-MU, G4Xp-MU) rather than given as machine-readable chemical structures.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are stated where measurements appear - molecular weights in kilodaltons, the ~80 Dalton phosphate/sulfate mass shift, reaction timepoints in hours - but they appear on figure axes, not in any data file, so this pass is cosmetic.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL. This is a mechanistic study built on a handful of engineered constructs, a small panel of active-site point mutants, and mouse cohorts of the size typical for muscle histology - orders of magnitude below the ~1,500-row bar. I could not count an exact n because no counts are tabulated; the paper reports results as individual gels and curves.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~0.1 MB of article XML plus one supplementary PDF
a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially fits, because there is essentially nothing to load. This pass carries no information.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Not assessable in any meaningful way: with no download and no tabulated counts, there is nothing for the paper, an API and a file to disagree about.

a8_label_provenance.note: Provenance is clean in principle - the measurements are genuine wet-lab enzyme assays, NMR binding experiments and mouse phenotypes, not another model's predictions and not computed from the inputs. But the measurements are locked inside figure images, so good provenance does not rescue the candidate.

honest_claim_h3: No claim is possible: the paper publishes no machine-readable measurements, so no model could be trained or tested on it.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use protein sequence to predict which protein domains strip phosphate groups off sugars attached to cell-surface proteins.
plain_idea.train_on: The project I considered would show a model the amino-acid sequence (and optionally a predicted three-dimensional structure) of a protein domain, and ask whether it carries a working haloacid dehalogenase-type phosphatase site - the DXDXT/V motif this paper shows is active in dystroglycan. This paper contributes a handful of sequences at most; the real training data would have to come from elsewhere.
plain_idea.predict: Output: whether the domain removes phosphate from a sugar substrate, and how fast. Ground truth would be a laboratory enzyme assay measuring released phosphate or the fluorescent sugar products this paper uses (G4Xp-MU versus G4X-MU). In this paper those readouts exist only as figure panels.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Researchers studying dystroglycanopathies - inherited muscular dystrophies caused by faulty sugar chains on dystroglycan - would use it to guess which of the many uncharacterised human haloacid dehalogenase-family domains act on sugars. But this paper cannot supply the data, so the idea would have to be built on public enzyme databases instead.

ml_idea: The scientifically interesting hook - that the N-terminal domain of dystroglycan is itself a sugar phosphatase, a function nobody expected from a receptor - would make a nice prediction task (find other cell-surface domains with hidden haloacid dehalogenase phosphatase activity). But that project would be built almost entirely from public enzyme resources such as BRENDA, UniProt and the Protein Data Bank, with this paper contributing one or two validated examples at most. It is not a project about this dataset, because this paper has no dataset.

effort.compute_note: Not estimated: there is no data to process, so every compute figure would be fictional.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Read the data availability statement and count the tables in the full text. Both took one command: the statement says 'available in the main text or the supplementary materials', and the article contains zero tables. That killed it in a single step.

verdict_reason: A classic mechanistic biochemistry and mouse-genetics paper with no machine-readable data of any kind. Part A1 fails: the data availability statement points at the figures, the single supplementary file is a Materials-and-Methods PDF with Figures S1-S7, and there is no deposit in GEO, SRA, the Protein Data Bank, ProteomeXchange, Zenodo or Dryad. A2 fails for the same reason - zero tables in the article, so the prediction target would have to be digitised from gel images. A5 fails on scale: a few engineered mutants and small mouse cohorts, nowhere near the ~1,500-row bar. The biology is genuinely novel (a receptor that turns out to be its own sugar phosphatase), but novelty in the finding is not data for a model.
